title: 1956 Bell decree replayed: compulsory DRAM know-how transfer to entrants
idea: Use the tool a 1955 antitrust lawyer used on AT&T: make CHIPS awards and merger/JV approvals conditional on each incumbent DRAM maker delivering a mature-node (1y/1z-class) process binder (full recipe deck, integration flow, yield-learning history) plus 12-24 months of seconded integration engineers to qualified U.S. entrants at a capped royalty, as the 1956 consent decree forced Bell to license the transistor at nominal cost.
why: Tacit process know-how, not patents, is the 5-7-year entry barrier; a binder plus seconded engineers could cut an entrant's yield ramp from ~5 years to ~2 and add a third or fourth U.S.-sited DRAM supplier this decade.

title: Memory checkoff: invoice levy funds a shared precompetitive process lab
idea: Copy the 1930s-50s agricultural marketing orders (cotton, milk and beef checkoffs): a statutory 0.5% levy on the invoice value of DRAM sold into the U.S. (~$0.5B/yr) flows to an industry-governed lab that develops process modules (capacitor dielectrics, contact and wiring alternatives, test flows) and licenses every result to all levy payers on identical terms.
why: Pools precompetitive R&D no single entrant can fund; spreading ~$0.5B/yr of module development across all buyers could cut an entrant's process-development spend 30-50% and shorten time to a competitive node (capital intensity, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Series-M Memory Bonds: payroll-deduction savings bonds that finance fabs
idea: A 1955 Treasury official would reuse the Series E war-bond machine: small-denomination, government-guaranteed 'Memory Bonds' sold through payroll deduction and TreasuryDirect, with proceeds ring-fenced in a revolving fund that lends to U.S. memory fabs at the Treasury rate plus ~50 bp.
why: Capital intensity: depreciation and capital cost are ~55% of wafer cost; cutting a $15B fab's cost of capital from ~10% to ~5% lowers cost per wafer an estimated 15-20% and opens a new ~$10-20B retail capital pool.

title: Shadow memory lines: retainer-funded warm-standby DRAM capacity inside existing fabs
idea: The 1936-39 British shadow-factory scheme applied to memory: the government pays an annual retainer for a qualified DRAM flow (masks, recipes, spare tool sets, trained crew) installed inside existing logic or foundry fabs, run at 10-20% on low-margin parts, and contractually surged to full output within 90 days when a published shortage index trips.
why: Shortages last 12-24 months but new fabs take 3-5 years; pre-qualified dormant capacity could add ~5-10% of bit supply within a quarter for a retainer worth a few percent of one new fab.

title: Allied Memory Community: ECSC-style treaty pooling DRAM capacity and investment
idea: Model on the 1951 European Coal and Steel Community: the U.S., Japan, Korea, Taiwan and the EU create a supranational Memory High Authority that removes intra-bloc tariffs on DRAM, tools and materials, runs a joint fab-investment fund from a common levy, and has treaty power to apportion members' output pro rata during a declared supply emergency.
why: Replaces five competing national subsidy races with one coordinated build-out, avoiding duplicate fabs and synchronized overbuild; targets ~30% lower subsidy cost per added wafer and steadier allied supply.

title: Certificates of Necessity: twelve-month write-off for certified memory fab tools
idea: The 1950-59 Korean War certificates let defense plants amortize in 5 years instead of 20 and sparked a capacity boom; a 2026 version lets certified U.S. DRAM tool purchases be fully expensed within 12 months, aimed squarely at the depreciation line that is ~55% of DRAM wafer cost.
why: Front-loads tax shields, lowering after-tax cost of capital ~2-3 points (worth ~8-12% on cost per bit for a new fab) and recycling cash into the next tool set years earlier (fact 4, capital intensity).

title: CCC-style non-recourse inventory loans: a bust-cycle floor for entrants
idea: Borrow the 1930s-50s Commodity Credit Corporation loan: a qualified U.S. memory maker can pledge tested, packaged DRAM as collateral at a published loan rate per GB; if contract prices crash below that rate it forfeits the parts instead of repaying, and forfeited parts are donated to public research computing rather than stockpiled.
why: DRAM busts (2008, 2012, 2019, 2023) killed Qimonda, Elpida and others; a price floor makes entrants bankable through a downturn, narrowing their financing spread and letting 2-3 extra suppliers survive a full cycle.

title: Silver-bond trick: DRAM-price-indexed fab bonds that hedge hyperscaler buyers
idea: Like the 1980 Sunshine Mining silver-indexed bonds, a new fab issues debt whose coupon floats with a published DRAM contract-price index; hyperscalers and OEMs buy it as a natural hedge, since when memory is dear the coupon rises and so does the fab revenue that pays it.
why: Matches debt service to the memory cycle, so the fab can carry more leverage at a ~150-250 bp lower base rate, cutting capital cost per bit ~10% and giving buyers price protection without a futures exchange.

title: Manhattan parallel paths: four memory routes, each with a calutron leg
idea: As 1942-45 ran gaseous diffusion, calutrons and thermal diffusion in parallel, fund four physically different DRAM-class production routes to pilot volume simultaneously, each with a 'calutron leg' that ships deliberately inefficient but available-now product (large-cell versions on existing tools) while the elegant version matures, with kill/scale gates every 9 months.
why: If each route has ~30% odds, running four raises P(at least one at volume by 2030) to ~76%; the calutron legs put bits on the market 2-3 years before optimized processes would.

title: Fluidic self-assembly of micro-dielets turns ramp-stage defects into usable bits
idea: A 2100 assembler's view: dice early-ramp DRAM wafers into ~0.2 mm2 micro-dielets and tumble them in a carrier fluid over substrates with shape-matched recesses (Alien Technology's 1990s RFID fluidic self-assembly), seating millions per hour; only tested-good dielets are released, then rewired into full-capacity modules by a redistribution layer.
why: Poisson yield e^(-D*A) at a new fab's D0 ~1/cm2 is ~55% for a 60 mm2 die but >99% for 0.2 mm2, so a ramping fab sells ~40% more good silicon from month one instead of waiting ~18 months for defect learning.

title: Edge-field memory dielets: harvest the blank rim of logic wafers
idea: A 2100 engineer would never leave wafer area unexposed: logic foundries step a second, small 'edge reticle' carrying eDRAM dielets into the partial fields at the wafer rim that are currently scrapped, so every advanced-logic wafer also yields a few hundred tiny memory dielets for cache chiplets and buffers.
why: Recovers ~3-6% of the area of over a million advanced-logic wafers per month as incremental memory supply at near-zero marginal wafer cost and with no new cleanroom.

title: Hot-swap chamber pods: robots exchange process modules without tool downtime
idea: A 2100 fab borrows the 1950s quick-change jet-engine pod: deposition and etch chambers become sealed, pre-seasoned pods that autonomous mobile robots exchange in under 30 minutes, with cleaning and part replacement done offline in a central pod depot.
why: Raises tool availability from ~85% to ~95%, a ~10% capacity gain on existing fabs with no new building, worth roughly $1.5B of new capacity per $15B fab.

title: CCD memory revival: image-sensor fabs build bucket-brigade streaming RAM
idea: Build what the 1970s shipped before DRAM won (Fairchild's 1975 64-kb CCD memory): mature 40-65 nm image-sensor lines fabricate charge-coupled shift-register memory with no per-bit transistor or deep capacitor (~4F2), organized as many short multiplexed loops for in-order traffic such as LLM weight and KV-cache streaming.
why: Adds bit supply from non-DRAM fabs without EUV; roughly 10x less dense than 12 nm DRAM but on ~3x cheaper wafers, offloading the sequential share of AI memory traffic from scarce DRAM.

title: Point-to-point wiring era: sell DRAM as known-good bare die
idea: A 1955 engineer soldered parts straight to the chassis: DRAM makers sell wafer-level-burned-in, fully tested bare die directly to module and accelerator makers for flip-chip or chip-on-board attach, skipping BGA package substrates, OSAT assembly and package-level test.
why: Packaging and final test are ~10-20% of DRAM cost and OSAT/substrate capacity gates ramps; bare-die shipment frees that capacity and cuts ~10% cost per bit.

title: Rickover's hafnium: naval zirconium byproduct secures domestic high-k precursors
idea: The 1950s naval reactor program created industrial Zr/Hf separation with hafnium as a byproduct; contract today's U.S. nuclear-zirconium separation stream for domestic hafnium and zirconium metal and build TEMAHf/TEMAZr precursor synthesis beside it, with offtake agreements from memory fabs for ZrO2/HfO2 capacitor stacks and high-k gate layers.
why: Hafnium output is only ~70-90 t/yr and geographically concentrated; a domestic precursor chain removes a quiet chokepoint under every DRAM capacitor at trivial cost per bit (scarce-resource intensity).

title: TVA logic: site fabs on retiring coal plants' interconnects
idea: 1950s aluminum smelters went where TVA power already was; a 2100 engineer sees 2026's binding constraint as multi-year grid-interconnection queues and water permits, so retiring coal plants' switchyards, cooling-water rights and rail spurs are pre-certified as fab sites and their interconnect queue positions transferred to the fab.
why: Grid hookup and permitting sit on the critical path of a 3-5-year fab build; reusing existing interconnects could pull first wafers forward ~1.5-2.5 years per fab.

title: IBM's abandoned X-ray proximity litho, revived with compact storage rings
idea: Resume the 1970s-80s IBM/AT&T path: 1:1 proximity X-ray lithography at ~1 nm wavelength for the periodic DRAM array layers, lit by compact storage-ring or inverse-Compton sources that several suppliers could build, needing no reflective optics and offering very large depth of focus.
why: EUV has one supplier and DRAM needs 5-7 EUV layers; X-ray proximity printing of regular arrays could halve array-litho capex per layer and remove the single-supplier chokepoint (fact 4).

title: Packard-built Merlins: licensed second-source manufacture of mature fab tools
idea: As Packard license-built Rolls-Royce Merlins and Studebaker built GE J47s, governments pay incumbent toolmakers a license fee so a second U.S. manufacturer builds their mature designs (e.g., DUV immersion scanners, ALD and etch platforms) from the original drawings under joint quality control.
why: Tool lead times of 12-24 months gate fab ramps; a licensed second line roughly doubles supply of mature but scarce platforms and creates a non-single-point source without new invention.

title: Fab Mutual: an engineering insurer that buys down fab outage risk
idea: A 1955 plant engineer knew Factory Mutual, the insurer that cut industrial fire losses by writing and inspecting its own engineering standards; form a memory-fab mutual whose members get low premiums only if they meet its outage standards (seismic base isolation for litho bays, 30-minute power ride-through, contamination-event drills), with inspection and loss data pooled across members.
why: Earthquakes, power dips and contamination events periodically wipe out weeks of output (2011 Japan, the 2019 Yokkaichi outage, the 2021 Texas freeze); halving such losses adds ~1-3% effective annual bit supply and steadies prices.

title: All American Five accelerators: memory-type-agile packages ship with any DRAM
idea: The 1930s-50s All American Five radio ran on AC or DC mains; design AI accelerators with a dual memory PHY and package footprint that accepts HBM, GDDR7 or LPDDR5X, with firmware that retunes scheduling, so each production lot ships with whichever DRAM type is in supply.
why: HBM is the tightest segment (~3x wafer area per bit, 20-30% yield loss, fact 6); letting accelerators fall back to commodity DRAM types turns idle GDDR/LPDDR capacity into usable AI memory supply and blunts single-segment shortages.

title: Memory QPL: one neutral qualification every buyer must accept
idea: Use the 1950s military Qualified Products List model: a neutral lab runs a published qualification suite (retention, row-hammer thresholds, reliability, JEDEC compliance) on new DRAM suppliers, and hyperscalers and OEMs contractually accept QPL listing in place of each running a separate 12-18-month private qualification.
why: Qualification delay is a hidden 1-1.5-year barrier for new suppliers; a shared QPL brings new capacity to market about a year sooner and cuts duplicated qualification cost ~70%.

title: Mercury delay line reborn: fiber-loop recirculating memory for weight streaming
idea: A 1955 engineer's mercury delay line rebuilt with 2026 telecom glass: model weights circulate as WDM optical pulses in a spooled fiber loop with erbium amplification and periodic regeneration, and an IBM 650 SOAP-style compiler places each layer's weights in the loop so they arrive exactly when the token schedule needs them.
why: No wafer, capacitor or refresh: capacity = bandwidth x delay (~40 Tb/s x 100 us = ~500 MB per 20 km spool), built from the U.S.-strong fiber and amplifier supply chain to offload cyclic weight reads from HBM (facts 5, 6).

title: Head-per-track drum streams LLM weights at HBM-class bandwidth
idea: Revive the 1955 IBM 650 head-per-track drum: a glass-platter rotor read by fixed multi-channel head arrays (tape-drive-style heads built on AlTiC ceramic wafers) streams every stored weight once per revolution, matching LLM decode, which reads all weights once per token.
why: About 1,000 parallel channels x ~2.5 MB per track x 120 rev/s = ~300 GB/s from non-volatile magnetic media at cents per GB, with no silicon wafer in the storage medium; frees HBM for KV-cache.

title: Silicon-on-sapphire gain cells on the LED industry's idle sapphire
idea: Resume RCA's 1970s SOS process with 2026 thin-film control: grow ~50 nm device silicon on LED-grade sapphire (supplied by restarting stranded crystal-growth fleets such as GTAT's former Mesa, AZ furnaces) and build gain-cell DRAM whose insulating substrate removes the storage-node junction leakage behind the retention tail; launch through space and defense buyers who already pay for rad-hard SOS.
why: Substrate comes from an over-built sapphire chain instead of silicon CZ wafers and quartz crucibles, and removing substrate leakage targets ~10x longer retention, cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss (fact 3).

title: 1952 ferroelectric matrix rebuilt with SAW-filter lithium niobate wafers
idea: Bell Labs tried BaTiO3 matrix memory in 1952; source thin-film LiNbO3-on-insulator wafers from the RF-filter industry (billions of SAW/BAW filters a year) and pattern crossbars where each bit is a ferroelectric domain whose conductive domain wall is read non-destructively by a small current, with no access transistor.
why: No silicon wafer, no capacitor charge wall (fact 1), non-destructive read (fact 8) and ns switching with high endurance; capacity draws on RF-filter substrate supply in the U.S., Japan and Europe rather than DRAM fabs.

title: Williams tube meets multibeam columns: vacuum charge-storage memory without refresh
idea: Combine the 1947 Williams tube, GE's 1970s BEAMOS and the Tektronix bistable storage tube: thousands of parallel electron beams (from multibeam e-beam-litho columns) write and read charge spots on a metal-backed dielectric target, while a low-energy flood gun holds each spot at one of two secondary-emission-stable potentials so data persists without refresh.
why: Bit density is set by beam spot (~20 nm), not lithography or a wafer; no capacitor pillar or access-transistor leakage tail (facts 1, 3), and the vacuum hardware comes from outside the DRAM tool chain.

title: Microscopic vacuum triodes as zero-leakage DRAM access switches
idea: A 1955 tube engineer would shrink the triode: nanoscale vacuum-channel transistors (sharp emitter, ~30 nm gap, gate electrode) made by sacrificial-layer release on sapphire or quartz wafers serve as the access device of a 1T1C cell, so off-current is set by suppressed field emission rather than semiconductor junction leakage.
why: Attacks the <=13 fA leakage tail that forces refresh (fact 3): field-emission off-current falls exponentially with gate bias, aiming at refresh intervals of minutes, with no silicon wafer or doping steps.

title: Idle LED MOCVD reactors grow MoS2 gain cells on synthetic quartz
idea: A 2100 engineer's atomically thin channel on 1950s Bell Labs hydrothermal synthetic quartz: repurpose the thousands of LED MOCVD reactors idled by overcapacity to grow wafer-scale monolayer MoS2 directly on quartz wafers, then build 2T gain cells whose 1.8 eV, sub-1-nm channel gives very low off-current.
why: Uses stranded LED tool capital and a hydrothermally grown non-silicon substrate (no quartz crucibles), targeting long-retention cells and a tool base outside DRAM fab capex (facts 3, 4).

title: Bubble memory's heir: skyrmion racetracks on optical-isolator garnet wafers
idea: The 1970s bet on magnetic bubbles in garnet; with 2026 materials, write and shift skyrmions in thin magnetic multilayers on gadolinium-gallium-garnet wafers from the Faraday-isolator industry, forming dense shift-register tracks driven by ns current pulses for in-order data such as streamed weights and KV blocks.
why: Non-volatile, no capacitor or refresh, potentially sub-4F2 per bit with 3D tracks; made on a garnet substrate chain unrelated to DRAM wafers, offloading sequential traffic from DRAM.

title: 1970s holographic page memory stores read-mostly weights in photopolymer
idea: Revive the 1970s Bell/RCA holographic page store: write model weights as angle-multiplexed holograms in thick photopolymer or LiNbO3 media and read whole 1-Mbit pages in parallel onto a detector array, with acousto-optic deflectors selecting pages in microseconds in the order the inference schedule needs.
why: Volumetric density of ~TB/cm3 class and Tb/s per device for read-only weights, with no silicon wafer in the medium, so HBM/DRAM holds only activations and KV-cache (facts 5, 6).

title: Wound-capacitor memory: thin-film bit tape rolled into 3D cylinders
idea: A 1955 engineer's wound paper capacitor applied to memory: fabricate a thin-film memory array on meters of polyimide or steel-foil tape roll-to-roll, then wind it into a cylinder whose bitlines all exit at the end faces, where laser-patterned flame-sprayed (Schoop-process) metal contacts them as in film capacitors, giving thousands of layers without tiers or TSVs.
why: Attacks fact 2 (no manufacturable 3D cell): layer count comes from winding (~1,000 turns per cm of radius) instead of per-tier process steps, on roll-to-roll web lines instead of wafer fabs.

title: Electric-eye access: photoconductor cells switched by optical wordlines
idea: Borrow the 1955 photocell 'electric eye': each storage capacitor connects to its bitline through a wide-gap photoconductor that is insulating in the dark, and rows are selected by light pulses in waveguide wordlines fed by GaN microLEDs on the same sapphire wafer, replacing the ~3 V electrical wordline.
why: Dark current of a wide-gap photoconductor can sit far below transistor leakage (fact 3) and optical row select removes wordline CV2 energy (fact 10), on LED-fab sapphire rather than silicon.

title: Ultrasound-crystal straintronics: piezo strain flips nanomagnets at attojoule energy
idea: A 2100 engineer's write mechanism: pattern elliptical magnetostrictive nanomagnets on thinned PMN-PT single-crystal wafers from the medical-ultrasound transducer industry; a local voltage on the piezo substrate strains each magnet through a 90-degree rotation, and an overlying MTJ stack reads the state.
why: Write energy ~aJ-fJ versus DRAM's refresh plus CV2 costs (facts 3, 10), non-volatile with magnetic endurance, on a U.S.-grown piezo-crystal substrate rather than a silicon wafer.

title: Bimetal-thermostat memory: VO2 cells held mid-hysteresis on sapphire
idea: Inspired by the 1955 bimetal thermostat: epitaxial VO2 cells on sapphire wafers are held by a global substrate heater inside their ~68 C insulator-metal hysteresis loop so each cell keeps whichever phase it was last put in; a short current pulse sets metal, a row-level thin-film Peltier pulse resets insulator, and resistance is read non-destructively.
why: A static, refresh-free bit (fact 3) with non-destructive read (fact 8) and ns set switching; one global heater replaces per-bit refresh, and the substrate is sapphire rather than silicon.

title: Telephone-relay access: NEMS contact switches give zero-leakage 1T1C cells
idea: A 1955 telephone-exchange engineer's answer to leakage: replace the access transistor with a nanoscale electrostatic contact relay (a ~100 nm cantilever on fused-quartz wafers) whose open air gap passes essentially zero current, so stored charge leaks only through the capacitor dielectric.
why: Removes the junction/subthreshold leakage tail behind refresh (fact 3), aiming at retention of hours and near-zero refresh energy; contact wear must reach >10^12 cycles, so it first suits read-mostly capacity.

title: Georgia kaolin to sapphire: a domestic high-purity alumina substrate chain
idea: As 1950s Alcoa built U.S. Bayer-process capacity, build a chain from Georgia kaolin through acid-leach 5N high-purity alumina to sapphire boules and wafers, sized for non-silicon memory substrates (SOS, 2D-channel, vacuum and relay cells) and avoiding both Spruce Pine quartz and imported HPA.
why: Gives non-silicon memory routes a U.S.-sourced substrate with no quartz-crucible chokepoint; HPA is largely imported today, so this de-risks scarce-resource intensity for every sapphire-based route.

title: Kremer-style milestone prizes for DRAM-class memory without silicon wafers
idea: Like the 1959 Kremer prize for human-powered flight, a public-private fund posts escalating cash prizes ($10M, $50M, $200M) for the first independently verified non-silicon-wafer memory meeting staged gates: <=100 ns access and >=10^15 cycles, then >=1 Gb/cm2, then <=$5/GB at pilot volume.
why: Pays only for verified results, pulling university, startup and adjacent-industry teams (RF filters, LEDs, magnetics) into non-silicon memory at a fraction of grant cost per success.

title: Gauge blocks for fabs: reusable sapphire monitor wafers replace silicon
idea: A 1955 metrologist used permanent gauge blocks rather than consumables: replace the silicon monitor, dummy and test wafers that consume roughly a tenth of DRAM wafer starts with hard-coated sapphire or sintered-SiC monitor substrates that are stripped and reused hundreds of times, backed by in-situ sensors for the rest.
why: Frees ~10% of prime silicon wafer, polysilicon and crucible demand for product wafers and cuts consumable cost, without touching the DRAM process itself.

title: Project Tinkertoy edge risers stack ceramic memory tiles without TSVs
idea: The Navy's 1950-53 Project Tinkertoy stacked printed ceramic wafers joined by vertical riser wires along their edges; stack thinned sapphire- or ceramic-substrate memory tiles and route all signals through plated edge risers on the stack's side faces instead of through-silicon vias.
why: Avoids the HBM TSV tax (fact 6: ~3x wafer area per bit, 20-30% yield loss) because tiles need no via keep-out zones, and the tiles are non-silicon substrates.

title: Antiferromagnetic CuMnAs bits on gallium phosphide wafers
idea: A 2100 engineer's spin memory with no stray fields: grow epitaxial CuMnAs on GaP wafers from the LED/III-V substrate chain, switch the Neel vector with ns current pulses via staggered spin-orbit torque, and read it by anisotropic magnetoresistance in a crossbar.
why: Non-volatile, high endurance, immune to field disturb between neighbors and potentially THz-fast, on a non-silicon substrate; attacks refresh (fact 3) and row hammer (fact 9).

title: 1970s III-V heterojunction wells: AlGaAs-barrier charge storage in RF GaAs fabs
idea: What 1970s III-V labs could have built instead of silicon DRAM: store charge in a GaAs quantum well confined by AlGaAs band-offset barriers on semi-insulating GaAs wafers, accessed through a heterojunction FET, made in existing RF GaAs fabs that build phone power amplifiers.
why: Band-offset confinement plus a semi-insulating substrate removes the junction leakage path, targeting retention well beyond silicon's ~64 ms at room temperature, using RF-fab capacity outside DRAM (fact 3).

title: Alcoa's gallium trick: Bayer-liquor gallium feeds non-silicon memory substrates
idea: Alcoa recovered gallium from Bayer-process liquor in the 1940s-50s; restart ion-exchange gallium recovery at U.S. alumina refineries to supply GaAs, GaP and gadolinium-gallium-garnet substrates for non-silicon memory routes, breaking dependence on China's ~98% share of primary gallium.
why: Non-silicon memory substrates (III-V, garnet) would otherwise inherit a single-country gallium chokepoint; byproduct recovery supplies tens of tonnes per year at low incremental cost.
